extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method; practitioners assessing inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for judging inductive inferences, experimental design, and the legitimacy of scientific hypotheses; includes guidance on methods of agreement/difference, concomitant variations, probability, and limits of induction. Suitable for evaluating scientific arguments, natural experiments, and hypothesis formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple causes operate together, their effects compose according to the conditions of their interaction; duplication of a cause will generally increase the effect, but the increase may not be strictly proportional depending on immediate vs. remote effects and collocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish immediate and remote effects; doubling a cause may double the immediate collocation (e.g., two men raising a gun faster, two sparks affecting more particles) but the observed effect at a place/time may not double if a certain collocation already suffices. Consider time and place separation: duplicating with different time/place (pointing two guns, exploding a second barrel later) will double effect. Examples: gun/sparks, doses of medicine (aperient vs laudanum), and reducing some cases to heteropathic laws when remote effects differ in kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish collocating causes from prime movers
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes that merely produce the collocation necessary for a prime mover to act (or release a potential force) are not always subject to additive composition in the same way as prime movers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to cases where adding more of a collocating cause (e.g., additional men to position a gun, extra sparks) makes no further observable difference because the necessary collocation was already achieved. Analyze whether a cause is an enabling/collocating condition or the direct generator of the effect; this affects how magnitude changes with duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze means in natural experiments (validity of Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural instances that resemble controlled Method of Difference experiments may be misleading if the means by which the antecedent was produced have independent effects on the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the intermediate operations used by Nature or observers (e.g., clearing a canopy of clouds) to determine whether those operations could themselves influence the outcome (dew deposition, etc.). Natural 'experiments' often employ complex means we cannot fully analyze; such cases chiefly corroborate conclusions already reached by other methods rather than serve as decisive evidence on their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and limits of the Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cause varies alone while other factors remain constant, a corresponding variation in the effect provides strong evidence of connection; this method can single out influencing causes even amid complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concomitant variations to assign causal influence when one antecedent varies and the effect varies correspondingly (examples: appetite and cold; tides with positions of sun/moon; muscle growth with exercise). Beware when many influencing causes coexist with none predominant or when several are continually changing—then it's rarely possible to assign precise shares to individual causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observation and experiment for elementary laws; use deduction for complex combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation and experiment are the ultimate basis of all knowledge and suffice to discover elementary functions (e.g., nerve functions), but in complex combinations experimental methods may be illusory and must be supplemented by deductive reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For simple physiological or physical laws, rely on direct experiments and observations; for complex systems (medical treatments, politics, economics) use deduction to disentangle interacting causes that experiments cannot isolate. Recognize the scope where experiment is effective versus where it is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of scientific hypotheses: deduce consequences and compare with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis is legitimate if it can be shown capable of producing the same kind of effects as those ascribed to it by deducing consequences and comparing them to observed phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame hypotheses (e.g., Broussais's localization of fevers, Gilbert's earth as magnet, brain-as-voltaic-pile, Darwin's natural selection) so that they yield testable consequences; disproving follows from failed consequences. Legitimacy does not require immediate proof but conformity to the rules of hypothesis: internal coherence, capacity to produce the phenomena, and amenability to testing by consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate rules for Hypothesis from rules for Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses and inductive proofs have different standards: hypotheses are conjectural devices to open inquiry and need not be proved by induction immediately, while inductive rules govern conditions of proof and verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat bold conjectures (e.g., Darwin’s natural selection) as legitimate when they afford plausible mechanisms and testable consequences; do not fault such hypotheses for not yet being inductively proved. Evaluate them by their fruitfulness and testability rather than by immediate inductive verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require demonstrable same-law production before unifying distinct forces
rubrics_metrics.description: When attempting to generalize or merge distinct phenomena (e.g., gravity and cohesion) under a single cause, it is indispensable to show that the proposed cause can produce the phenomena according to the same law; otherwise the unity is merely nominal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether candidate unifying causes share essential laws (e.g., range, dependence on distance, variability) and actually simplify explanation. Avoid superficial unifications that ignore substantial differences in manner of action (e.g., gravity's inverse-square and cohesion's rapid fall-off).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate central tendency and estimation for inductive inquiry (mean vs average)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inductive purposes the true 'mean' is not always the simple arithmetic average when deviations are asymmetric; the most probable determination of invariable elements minimizes the sum of the squares of individual deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating invariable elements from observations, use principles like least squares (minimize sum of squared deviations) rather than naive averaging when distributions are skewed or when deviations differ in magnitude and frequency. Refer to Quetelet/Herschel explanations for probabilistic grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability assessment requires defined sample space and causal grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculating chances depends on a well-defined enumeration of possibilities and knowledge of their relative frequencies; without experience-based data or a principled way to list possibilities, probability calculations often break down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply simple enumerative chance models when possibilities are not clearly delimited (e.g., 'all possible colors' vs a few chosen colors). The first observed instance is uniquely important because it establishes possibility; subsequent instances inform about intensity, extent, and stability of the cause. Always ground probability in causal understanding and empirical frequency where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat empirical regularities as conditional on constancy of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: An empirical law or event that has never failed within observed trials is 'certain' only as long as the same collocation of causes continues; probability theory cannot predict if underlying causes subsequently change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret observed certainty as conditional certainty: if the collocation of causes remains unchanged, the regularity holds. Recognize that a sudden failure indicates a change in collocation; probabilities cannot account for unforeseen changes in causes beyond the scope of recorded observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware incomplete instance-recitals in social and economic 'proofs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitals of instances used to prove economic or political doctrines are often futile if circumstances of the cases are not fully stated; selective omission and lack of contextual detail render such evidence inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating historical or anecdotal evidence (e.g., attempts to prove economic doctrines by example, or that announcement of a diplomatic rupture immediately deranged markets), require full statement of circumstances and control for omitted counter-instances. Treat such single 'experiments' as verifications of deductions only if supported by broader motive-based understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit tentative hypotheses in emerging fields but acknowledge verification difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: In nascent sciences, formulating tentative hypotheses (e.g., phrenology's localization attempts) is legitimate as a starting method, but one must recognize the limited grounds and the practical difficulties involved in their verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept initial, bold, or tentative conjectures as part of inquiry (they can guide research), but maintain critical awareness of the sparse evidence base. Avoid presenting such tentative theories as established science; emphasize their provisional nature and the need for rigorous methods to test them.
